This a first draft version :
PANTS is a proposal for an open-source dataset for pancreatic CT scans.
A major limitation of existing public tumor datasets is the lack of normal scans, which prevents reliable evaluation of AI sensitivity and leads to inflated false-positive rates in population screening where disease prevalence is very low. PanTS addresses this by including a large proportion of normal scans (~80%) with clinical follow-up and both contrast-enhanced and non-contrast CTs, supporting more realistic screening and generalization studies.

Equally important is the availability of metadata, which enables risk stratification. By combining imaging, biomarkers, and clinical information, AI can be applied to higher-risk cohorts, substantially improving positive predictive value and clinical utility. Unlike many public datasets, PanTS provides metadata such as patient age, imaging protocols, and annotated biomarkers, making it a more useful resource for developing clinically relevant early detection models.

The PanTS proposal introduces what is described as the largest and most comprehensive dataset for pancreatic CT to date, containing 36,390 scans—over 12 times larger than the next-largest public dataset. The dataset includes expert-validated with , voxel-wise annotations of tumors, pancreatic sub-regions,  (a complete set of 28 masks for every scan created by a group of 23 radiologist annotators). Its design emphasizes out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation, with training data drawn from 11 public datasets and testing from 3 independent institutions. Experiments show that PanTS substantially improves performance on downstream tasks, including a marked increase in OOD detection performance (AUC from 0.819 to 0.959) and a notable gain in tumor segmentation accuracy when anatomical context is included. Inter-annotator agreement analysis and ablation studies further strengthen the evidence for the dataset’s design choices. The dataset reportedly covers 145 medical centers across 20 countries, and both dataset and code (well documented) are made available on Hugging Face and GitHub.

Limitations : 

The dataset focuses primarily on segmentation tasks and pays less attention to clinically actionable applications, such as staging or surgical planning. However, the provided material may be valuable for these applications.
While OOD testing is emphasized, the test set is limited to academic medical centers, raising questions about broader representativeness. 
Claims of geographic and pathological diversity are not supported by quantitative breakdowns—details on patient demographics, race, ethnicity, and tumor type prevalence are absent. 
Key aspects of dataset curation and annotation procedures are insufficiently described, including consistency of annotations across all structures, metadata on collection sites and scanners, the process for resolving annotator disagreements, and whether multiple annotations per scan exist. 
The evaluation is limited to nnU-Net, which is pertinent for the task, though it is debatable.

To date though, accessibility is incomplete, as model weights are unavailable and dataset usage instructions are lacking.

Dear All Reviewers,

Thanks for your encouraging words and recognizing our contribution. Your comments have guided our latest updates and future plans to enhance the impact of the PanTS dataset. Below, we summarize key updates and directions based on your suggestions:

---

**1 | Normal scans matter!**

The lack of pathology-proven normal scans is a serious but undervalued problem in public tumor datasets. For example, all the data in MSD-Pancreas contain pancreatic tumors, so we won't know if the AI is overly sensitive. No test can be done on normal scans. Similarly, KiTS (for kidney tumors) and LiTS (for liver tumors) datasets also offer a very limited number of normal scans.

But the truth is, in a general population screening context where PDAC prevalence is extremely low (~0.1%), even a highly accurate model will yield a low positive predictive value (PPV). Bayesian analysis estimates this: applying our best AI model to 100,000 individuals results in ~1,096 positive predictions, but only 97 are true positives—meaning over 90% of AI-flagged cases are false positives. This leads to unnecessary anxiety, overdiagnosis, and costly follow-ups.

The PanTS dataset offers a large number of normal scans (~80%) that had at least two years of clinical follow-up. These scans span both contrast-enhanced (e.g., venous, arterial, delayed) and non-contrast CTs. Notably, over 14% of our test set comprises non-contrast scans, enabling evaluation in opportunistic screening settings where imaging was not initially intended for cancer detection.

**We plan to continue curating normal scans with either: (1) no pancreatic tumor, or (2) no tumor in any organ.**

---

**2 | Metadata matters!**

The current AI is not ready for screening in a general population as discussed above. But if we leverage a medical knowledge graph to select high-risk individuals—using deep networks, imaging biomarkers, clinical notes—the prevalence of pancreatic tumors in the tested cohort increases substantially, improving PPV and making AI far more clinically useful. For example, in high-risk populations where prevalence is closer to 4.4% (e.g., 1 in 23), the PPV of our AI model rises to over 74%, transforming it from a blunt population-level screener into a precision detection tool. Thus, integrating risk stratification is critical to realizing the full potential of AI for early tumor detection. Unfortunately, public datasets (e.g., MSD-Pancreas) often do not release the metadata with CT scans.

The PanTS dataset offers patient metadata information (e.g., age), imaging protocols (e.g., contrast phase), and imaging biomarkers (e.g., annotated duct) to help develop models to identify high-risk individuals. 

**We have already released the PanTS metadata spreadsheet on Hugging Face.**

With sincere appreciation,

The PanTS Team

Dear Reviewers, ACs, and PCs,

Thank you sincerely for your thoughtful feedback, questions, and suggestions. We truly appreciate the time and care you put into reviewing our work.

As you’ve noted, PanTS (Pancreatic Tumor Segmentation Dataset) represents a major step forward for the field. Inspired by landmark datasets like BraTS, LiTS, and KiTS, PanTS is the largest and most comprehensive **open-source** dataset for pancreatic CT analysis to date—comprising **36,390** 3D scans from **145** medical centers across **20** countries, with expert-validated, voxel-wise annotations covering 28 anatomical structures per scan, including tumors, pancreas subregions, and surrounding vessels and organs.

We have made the dataset, code, and documentation openly available to the community at GitHub: `MrGiovanni/PanTS` and Hugging Face: `BodyMaps/PanTSMini`.

Our goal is to make PanTS a lasting, high-impact benchmark that enables robust, reproducible AI research and supports a broad range of downstream clinical applications—from tumor segmentation to staging, surgical planning, radiomics, and education.

If there are any remaining concerns, clarifications, or suggestions you’d like us to address, we would be more than happy to respond.

With sincere appreciation,

The PanTS Team

rebuttal.value:
> **Q1.** *Are the 24 structures and pancreatic tumors annotated consistently in each example? In other words, is there any missing data?*

- No missing data. Every scan has a full 28‑class mask—tumor and 27 organs or vessels—as described in `Lines 108‑113`, `Figure 1B–D` and `Figure  3A–D`.

---

> **Q2.** *How was the dataset collected? Was data collection done specifically for the manuscript? They collection protocol may affect segmentation quality etc.*

- 27 % (9,901 CT scans) came from 11 public abdominal CT datasets; we re-annotated pancreatic tumors and 27 organs or vessels in all these scans (see `Appendix C` for the annotation standards). 

- 73 % (26,489 CT scans) were specifically collected and annotated for this study under IRB 00403268. This followed the following collection protocol:

  - *Inclusion criteria:* contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans covering the pancreas, with lesions confirmed by surgical or biopsy pathology. Normal control cases had at least two years of clinical follow-up.

  - *Exclusion criteria:* Low-quality images (e.g., significant artifacts or patient motion) were excluded.

---

> **Q3.** *If the dataset was collected in 145 medical centers, will information about each site and acquisition device (e.g., CT scanner model) used to collect data be available as meta-data for each example?*

- Yes, we will provide metadata of de‑identified *145 medical centers*, *acquisition device* (e.g., CT scanner, voxel spacing, slice thickness, and contrast phase), and *patient information* (e.g., patient age and sex) for every scan.

---

> **Q4.** *What procedure was used to sequester the training and testing dataset?*

- We split the dataset by medical centers. All 142 centers from public data were assigned to the training set, while UCSF, UW, and PUTH were reserved for the test set. This split helps prevent patient and protocol overlap between training and testing. Details are provided in `Section 3.2` and the caption of `Figure 2`.

---

> **Q5.** *For annotator disagreement, authors state "In cases of disagreement, a specialist served as the final arbiter to resolve labeling conflict". What is the process the labelling conflicts were resolved?*

- In cases of disagreement between annotators, a senior radiologist specialized in pancreatic imaging reviewed the case and served as the final arbiter. This radiologist carefully examined both annotations and manually created a single consensus annotation by editing and reconciling the differences. This process ensured high-quality and clinically reliable labels.

---

> **Q6.** *Do any examples contain annotations from multiple annotators, or does each CT scan contain only a single annotation mask?*

- During the dataset creation process, 300 CT scans were annotated independently by two junior radiologists. 

  - When two junior radiologists agree on the annotations but have small differences, such as slightly different boundaries, we combine their annotations by averaging them. This helps reduce minor differences and creates a smooth, consistent final mask.

  - For the small fraction of cases with disagreement (about 4%), a senior radiologist, specialized to the pancreas, reviewed the scan and provided a final consensus annotation. 

- In the released dataset, we include only the final consensus annotation for each scan. That said, each CT scan has a single annotation mask.

> **Q1.** *Lack of Quantitative Diversity Data: This is the most significant weakness. The paper claims broad geographic diversity (145 centers, 20 countries) but provides no quantitative breakdown of the number of scans per country. Furthermore, no data on patient race or ethnicity is presented, making the claims of diversity and fairness difficult to assess rigorously.*

- The geographic diversity of the dataset is already shown in `Figure 2` where the circle size on the world map reflects the number of scans per country.

- More concretely, the exact scan counts from each of the 20 countries are listed in the table below. We will include and discuss this table in the camera-ready version.

- Race and ethnicity: Due to HIPAA and data protection laws in several EU countries, we cannot release race or ethnicity information in multi-institutional imaging datasets. These fields are also not present in the raw DICOM headers. However, since our dataset includes scans from many countries—with varying ethnic backgrounds—it already reflects some demographic diversity. In addition, we will release age histograms and sex distributions (see `Table 1`), and we will describe these safeguards in the Ethics Appendix of the camera-ready version.

This makes it difficult for users to know if the dataset is suitable for studying specific or rare tumor subtypes.*

- PanTS was created for tumor segmentation, not specifically for tumor sub-type classification. The CT scans in the training set come from public datasets, which do not include pathology results or radiology reports—so we don’t know the tumor sub-types for those cases. rebuttal.value:
> **Q1.** *Only segmentation tasks seem to be limited. The tumor staging or surgical assessment might be better to give actionable utility in the clinic.*

- Segmentation is often the first and most essential step for many downstream clinical tasks. PanTS gives a complete set of 28 masks for every scan, including tumor, pancreas head/body/tail, and 24 nearby vessels and organs (`Lines 108-113`; `Figure 1B-D`; `Figure 3A-D`). We hope this dataset will support a wide range of clinical applications and educational use cases. For example,

  - *Tumor staging and surgical planning:* Tumor size and vessel involvement can be directly measured from the segmentation masks using simple, rule-based algorithms. This enables automated assessment of tumor stage and resectability in just a few lines of code (e.g., P. Bassi et al., ICCV 2025, arXiv:2501.04678).

  - *Radiotherapy dose planning:* Segmentation masks for organs at risk are included in PanTS, allowing researchers to test radiation planning strategies without needing manual contouring.

  - *Radiomics research:* With over 1,000,000 segmentation masks, researchers can compute a wide variety of radiomic features. Radiomics has already been shown to predict early signs of pancreatic cancer in pre-diagnostic scans (S. Mukherjee et al., Gastroenterology, 2022, doi: 10.1053/j.gastro.2022.06.066).

  - *Medical education:* Students and trainees can overlay the anatomical masks on CT scans and compare them with their own annotations, providing a valuable learning tool.

---

> **Q2.** *The test set is claimed to be 'out-of-distribution' but seems like only UCSF, UW, PUTH. All of these are still academic medical centers so the underlying distribution might not be representative.*

- Sorry for the confusion. In our paper, the terminology “UCSF,” “UW,” and “PUTH” refer not only to academic medical centers, but to the broader data sources—comprising both academic and clinical hospitals—affiliated with each institution. Let us clarify:

  1. *UW* refers to a national dataset of pancreatic CT scans from across Poland. The dataset is named “UW” because it was organized by contributors at the University of Warsaw. However, the scans were collected from multiple clinical sites across the country, making the dataset representative of Poland’s broader healthcare system.

  2. *UCSF* includes CT scans collected from a network of affiliated hospitals across California, not just from UCSF Academic Medical Center. We use the term “UCSF” as a shorthand because, again, they were organized by contributors at UCSF.

  3. *PUTH* is a public tertiary Grade 3A general hospital in China. It is a large clinical institution and should not be considered only within an academic context.

- To prevent further confusion, we will revise the terminology in the camera-ready version and may refer to these datasets more generically (e.g., Dataset A, B, and C).

- It is "out-of-distribution" because none of these sources—UW, UCSF, or PUTH—appear in the training set. There are clear distributional differences between the training and testing sets (see `Table 1`). For example,
  - *Contrast Usage:* 15% of test scans are non-contrast, compared to only 7.9% in the training set.
  - *Hounsfield Unit Distributions:* The mean Hounsfield unit distributions differ by more than 1.5 standard deviations between the training and test sets—a common out-of-distribution sign.


---

> **Q3.** *The universal DSC>20% threshold might not be cancer specific and that can make it hard to distinguish larger tumor and smaller tumor.*

- We use DSC score here to measure how much two radiologists disagree when they annotate the same tumor—not to evaluate AI performance. If the DSC is below 20%, which means the two annotations are very different, a senior radiologist reviews and updates the annotation. This process is shown in `Figure 4`.

- We agree that DSC does not always capture differences well, especially between large and small tumors. For example, small tumors often have lower DSC scores even if the annotations are clinically reasonable. As noted in `Line 188`, we found that most cases revised by senior radiologists involved small or ambiguous tumors. This is expected, as large tumors tend to have clearer boundaries, leading to higher agreement between radiologists.

- Thanks to your insightful comment, we are exploring better ways to measure inter-radiologist agreement beyond DSC. One alternative we are considering is the *95th percentile Hausdorff distance*, which may better capture boundary differences. We would appreciate your thoughts or suggestions on this.

---

> **Q4.** *For modeling, only nnU-Net is evaluated. More modern transformer based models or other VLMs are missing or not discussed.*

- In `Figure 5B` and `Appendix B.1`, we have compared PanTS-trained nnU-Net with several strong baseline models that have ranked among the top performers in the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) challenge. These baseline models include:
  1. modern transformer-based models (i.e., Swin UNETR)
  2. vision-language models (i.e., Universal Model)
  3. neural architectural search framework (i.e., DiNTS, C2FNAS). 

- As a dataset team, we are not ideally positioned to fairly benchmark externally developed AI models, especially those re-implemented by us. This concern has been echoed in recent benchmarking studies:

  - nnU-Net Revisited (Isensee et al., MICCAI 2024, arXiv:2404.09556, `Table 1`) shows that nnU-Net consistently matches or outperforms recent transformer-based and Mamba-based models across diverse medical segmentation tasks.
  - Touchstone Benchmark (Bassi et al., NeurIPS 2024, arXiv:2411.03670, `Tables 2–3`) also finds that nnU-Net performs on par with or better than state-of-the-art transformers (e.g., MedFormer) and significantly outperforms recent vision-language and SAM-based models. 

- These results further support our choice of nnU-Net as a strong and reproducible baseline.

- Based on your valuable suggestion, we have invited the inventors of several state-of-the-art AI models—including *MedFormer* (top performer in Touchstone), and *3D TransUNet* (a widely cited transformer model for medical segmentation). These researchers are independently benchmarking their models on the PanTS dataset. The results will be made publicly available on the official PanTS GitHub page.

---

> **Q5.** *The dataset seems to be on HF. The code is pretty well documented (kudos for split info attention). But I cant seem to find the model weights.*

- Thanks for your praise. The model weights will be publicly available once this paper gets accepted.

summary.value: This paper introduces PanTS, a large-scale, multi-institutional CT dataset designed to advance automated pancreatic cancer analysis. Containing 36,390 scans from 145 medical centers, it addresses the limitations of small, homogeneous public datasets. The primary contributions are twofold: first, the dataset itself, featuring expert-validated, voxel-wise annotations of tumors, pancreatic sub-regions, and 24 surrounding anatomical structures; second, extensive experiments demonstrating that models trained on PanTS achieve significantly improved performance on downstream tasks, especially on out-of-distribution (OOD) data, thereby establishing a new benchmark for the field.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Transformative Scale and Clinical Relevance: With 36,390 CT scans, PanTS is over 12 times larger than the next-largest public dataset.

2. Rigorous Dataset Design and Curation: The methodology is a key strength. The train/test split is explicitly designed to test out-of-distribution generalization, using 11 public datasets for training and 3 entirely new institutions for testing. 

3. Compelling Experimental Validation: The paper provides powerful evidence for its design choices. Experiments show that the scale and quality of PanTS lead to a dramatic leap in OOD detection performance (AUC from 0.819 to 0.959). Including anatomical context (28-class model) improves tumor segmentation DSC by +10.3% over a basic 2-class model.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Lack of Quantitative Diversity Data: This is the most significant weakness. The paper claims broad geographic diversity (145 centers, 20 countries) but provides no quantitative breakdown of the number of scans per country. Furthermore, no data on patient race or ethnicity is presented, making the claims of diversity and fairness difficult to assess rigorously.

2. Unquantified Diversity of Tumor Types: The paper states that PanTS includes a "broad spectrum of pancreatic tumor types" (e.g., PDAC, PNETs) but offers no statistics on the prevalence of these different pathologies. This makes it difficult for users to know if the dataset is suitable for studying specific or rare tumor subtypes.

title.value: PanTS: The Pancreatic Tumor Segmentation Dataset

abstract.value: PanTS is a large-scale, multi-institutional dataset curated to advance research in pancreatic CT analysis. It contains 36,390 CT scans from 145 medical centers, with expert-validated, voxel-wise annotations of over 993,000 anatomical structures, covering pancreatic tumors, pancreas head, body, and tail, and 24 surrounding anatomical structures such as vascular/skeletal structures and abdominal/thoracic organs. Each scan includes metadata such as patient age, sex, diagnosis, contrast phase, in-plane spacing, slice thickness, etc. AI models trained on PanTS achieve significantly better performance in pancreatic tumor detection, localization, and segmentation than those trained on existing public datasets. Our analysis indicates that these gains are directly attributable to the 16× larger-scale tumor annotations and indirectly supported by the 24 additional surrounding anatomical structures. As the largest and most comprehensive resource of its kind, PanTS offers a new benchmark for developing and evaluating AI models in pancreatic CT analysis.
